This is not dissimilar to what people are already doing in some probabilistic programming languages. For instance, look at the following two articles. 

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.09089v1.pdf

http://ijcai.org/Abstract/15/391 


Just based on these papers, the key difference is that they are then constructing a learner for the posterior distributions for this framework (but I was under the impression this is widely studied in PP), and they run this learner and show that the approach performs so well. So there's nothing inherently wrong as far as I could see in the submission, but I just didn't see it to be very surprising or with new ideas. As I mentioned, I  cannot comment on the novelty of the learning, because I do not know the latest in terms of the learning of  the posterior distributions of probabilistic programs. Perhaps some other reviewer can comment on that.

**Summary Of Contributions:**

I should point out that although I'm familiar  with the literature on probabilistic programming, my background is more on the side of logical inference, so perhaps closer to things like probabilistic logic programming and weighted-model counting. So I may not be the most appropriate reviewer to appreciate this submission, although as I said, I'm familiar with the motivations and the background for probabilistic programming. 

Now, having said that, I don't find the paper to be contributing something new. Perhaps I'm missing what's so surprising or unique about the approach. Let me quickly summarize what they try to do. They  take program descriptions from the probabilistic program, and they construct a sampler that respects some of the instructions in the probabilistic program. 

**Requested Changes:**
- articulate better what the differences are from papers referred to above

I can understand if the answer is something like: "although the idea of constructing a sampler based on program primitives is not new (e.g., 1, 2), the exploration of these concepts for X and Y along with a generic learning scheme for posteriors hasn't been explored before, and this is what we show."

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
making PP inference easy to access would enable a more principled ML building process

To the best of my knowledge, the authors' claim that this is the first work to consider applying neural networks to probabilistic programming is correct. There is indeed substantial work on using neural networks for general purpose computational tasks, but not specifically the kind of probabilistic inference tasks considered here. It is also correct that probabilistic inference is, in general, a hard problem for which most existing methods are not entirely satisfactory, and that the proposed method seems to compute results considerably faster in some cases. I also appreciated that the work considered the ability of the trained networks to generalize beyond the sampled program distribution, to hold-out structures, as this tends to be the achilles' heel of neural methods.

That said, I think the main weakness of the work is that (1) the approach is rather straightforward -- it's only the particular type of computation that is novel here -- and more significantly (2) the results of these experiments are rather mixed -- the losses diverge as training is lengthened for a nonnegligible number of test programs on the various experiments -- and there does not seem to be much insight as to whether this is inherent, or simply due to the particulars of the methodology used in these experiments. I appreciate that one of the main motivations of this work was to improve computational efficiency, but there is a distinction between the resources involved in training and the resources involved in performing inference using the trained representations -- indeed, the generation of samples for training using existing methods is quite expensive already. But, the network blocks used are rather small, whereas the "unreasonable effectiveness" of current training methods only kick in when relatively large numbers of units are used; although this may seem to be at odds with the stated objective of obtaining a small network for performing inference at the end, the standard approach is to use distillation -- treating the penultimate layers' activation as a target for regression by a smaller network -- which seems to retain the benefit of training with a large network while producing a small representation to reduce the size of the output. Again, this is all standard by now. So, the work does not address the question of whether or not we would obtain more favorable results by the now-standard methodology for training neural networks. (And, yes, the feasibility of this generally requires making use of GPUs for training.) 

As an aside, I was also concerned about the lack of quantification at certain key points, specifically how many test programs diverged (the text says "a few" out of 50, but on that scale the number seems significant), and how accurate the distributions are. Visual inspection of the curves is hard, especially when the plots are so small as to be essentially unreadable. I agree that the KL-divergence would be ideal and acknowledge that it is hard to estimate, but other metrics, such as the l1 difference between the densities, would still be helpful.

Finally, the 12-page "body" does not stand on its own. I needed to read the appendices to even see most of the results.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
The paper proposes to learn a method for computing marginals and sampling for probabilistic programming. The approach is to train neural networks to compute updates to a sample and likelihood estimate corresponding to the operations in a simple straight-line probabilistic programming language, represented by a learned internal state. Once trained, these networks may be composed to represent a new probabilistic program in the language; the final output of the program is obtained by applying a final decoder network to the output of the network corresponding to the final instruction. This approach is evaluated against an existing method, HMC, for computing samples and estimating marginals. The experiments test the ability to generalize to parameters for new models drawn from the same training distribution; generalization to a hold-out model structure; and the speed of producing samples via importance sampling with the new method. The main advantage of the new method is claimed to be primarily computational.

**Requested Changes:**
We need some sense of whether training using larger/deeper network blocks would address the issues with the approach, specifically whether or not the resulting program representations would become suitably accurate with sufficient training time. If not, it would at least serve as a negative finding. As it stands, these results seem too preliminary for publication.

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
I'm not concerned about the ethical implications of this work.

The paper partially succeeds in making the importance of the topics clear.
It isn't fully clear from abstract and introduction what is the exact contribution of the paper.
The text is hard to understand (see below for a small sample of difficulties).  After section 3, it isn't fully clear hwat are the probability distributions under consideration, what is the semantics of the programs, what posterior is inferred, why this is difficult with existing methods, what is a "state", how the complex neural networks fits in there, how states and posterior distributions are encoded, etc.  As a result, at that point the reader doesn't feel sufficiently prepared to read the actual contribution in Section 4.
The use of English language is fair but contains many minor mistakes, e.g., missing articles and incorrect singulars/plurals.
The text lists limitations of the approach and future work, but doesn't give many ideas on how we could in future let such approach scale better.


Detailed comments:

- Section 1 uses many terms without introducing them.  This may be acceptable if (a) non-experts get another way to learn about these concepts, e.g., in the preliminaries section, and (b) non-experts get at least a high-level impression of the problem and the contribution already in the introduction.  at least The latter of those conditions is in my opinion insufficiently satisfied.
- Section 2: ... supports basic forms of expression and conditional statement -> ... statements.
- The grammar provided in the beginning of Section 2 seems incomplete.  e.g., in the text says $v_0$ and $v_1$ are reals, but if so then the rule $v0 := v1$ doesn't make much sense.  Probably you mean that you can substitute a numerical expression v_0 can be a variable name z.  If $z$ is not just a real but the name of a variable, also $z\sim\mathcal{N}(v_0,v_1)$ would make more sense.
- "We permit only the programs where a variable does not appear more than once on the left-hand side of the := and ∼ symbols. This means that no variable is updated twice or more." -> do you mean "defined" rather than "updated"?
- "The choice of the target PPL is intended. ... While having the important merit," -> Please specify which merit "the merit" is referencing.
- "We permit only the programs where a variable does not appear more than once on the left-hand side of the ... " --> In fact, this characterization probable doesn't exclude all undesired programs.  E.g., I imagine also the program $z_1\sim \mathcal{N)(z_2,1); z_2\sim\mathcal{N}(z_1,20)$ would be problematic (cyclic dependency) ?   In fact, the syntax as provided in the text here doesn't provide a semantics.  Even reading appendix C leaves questions, e.g., when the text says $P(z_{1:n})=P(x_{1:m}|z_{1:n}).\prod_i P(z_i|z_{1:i-1})$ the use of the term "posterior" gets unclear.  Usually, one provides a probability distribution (prior), and "observations" form evidence from which one can compute the posterior.  However, it seems the prior is simply $\prod_i P(z_i|z_{1:i-1})$ and the formula above already gives the posterior.  If so, it is unclear why a complex approach is needed to infer the posterior.   Appendix C also talks about "update" variables (top page 18) while the fact that every variable only occurs once on the lefthandside of a $\sim$ suggests values are only drawn once and never updated in the course of a program.  In the end, I fail to understand the semantics explained in appendix C, e.g., on top of page 18 the text mentions "non-sample" statements (it's the only time this term is used), it is unclear which statements are meant and what is their semantics.
- Section 3: $h_0\in\mathbb{R}^s$ -> please remind the reader of the meaning of $s$.  Is $s$ related to the number of atomic commands $k$, the number of $z$ variables $n$ or the number of $x$ variable $m$ ?  What is the meaning of a state h_0 ?
- $Z_0$ is a marginal likelihood, but of what event is it the marginal likelihood?
- "Formally, our inference algorithm is built on top of three kinds of neural networks: ..." : the text gives three types of neural networks, but at this point the reader does not know yet what it means "to transform the state h" (i.e., how the state should be transformed) etc.
- "and use at most $m$-many variables (so $m\ge n$)." -> above, the text said there are $n$ variables $z_1 .. z_n$ and $m$ variables $x_1 ... x_m$, which makes the algorithm already use $m+n$ variables (more than $m$).  It is unclear why $m\ge n$ is needed.  
- $[0,1]^m$ is not a space of one-hot encodings but a space of all possible bit vectors
- The text doesn't seem very explicit on what are "procedures".  Are these simple the operators +, -, *, / etc which take 2 reals and output another real?  Why aren't there unary procedures such as -, sqrt, log, etc.?
- Around here several times the notation x_{i:j} is used. Usually this means a subrange of a vector, but maybe here you intend a universal quantifier?
- "the last neural network computes ..." : in the integral we see $\mathcal{N}(r;v_0,v_1)$ but $\mathcal{N}$ usually takes only two parameters (mean and variance).
- please specify the semantics of "let x=y in z".  For example, in several cases I don't see x occurring in z so the interpretation "substitute x by y in z" doesn't seem the correct interpretation.
- It isn't clear why exactly the algorithm is called "white box".  How would a black box look like?
- What is the meaning of "meta" here?  Usually, meta-learning means that existing learning algorithms exist and one learns which one to use.  Here it seems you directly learn the parameters of the many neural networks, but don't start from existing good inference algorithms.
- It is unclear how to efficiently compute the loss function at the top of page 6.  The text mentions sampling as a strategy to get posterior samples, so maybe some sampling strategy is used there too.  Insufficient details are present to reproduce the results, e.g., how many samples are used?   It seems also important to empirically investigate how the computational cost scale with the size of the problem.
- The empirical evaluation would benefit from more details to make it reproducible.  E.g., appendix E describe a random PPL generator.  Still, how many instances are generated?  Also, Appendix E gives programs with parameters and explains the parameters are randomly sampled, but then the question remains how we get training examples with the atomic commands in different orders?  
- In Appendix C, please explain what is meant with update, concentration operator, judgement, rule (probably two expressions separated by a horizontal line?), etc.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
The paper presents an approach to learn neural networks which can be used to transform a probabilistic program into a posterior distribution.  The paper explains the probabilistic programs and the learning strategy, and presents experiments.

**Requested Changes:**
It is imperative to rewrite the text much more clearly.  Only when the text is fully understandable it will become possible to make a full list of changes which are necessary.  At least, it seems important to discuss relationships with existing work (e.g., how does this method compare to existing hardcoded inference algorithms?), to provide all details required to achieve reproducibility, and to provide a more systematic experimental evaluation.

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
I have no ethical concerns about this paper.

The approach is novel, quite interesting, and supported by the right experiments. I'm rather skeptical that it will scale, but the authors don't claim that, so there's no issue here.

I have a few questions about Section 5.3. First of all, it looks like HMC is performing poorly, much worse than even IS from the prior. Is it perhaps because the example programs chosen (which would be nice to see in the main text) are inherently difficult for HMC? It makes me a little suspicious about whether the evaluation is fair. I would expect a mixed bag of results, with IS-pred sometimes being better than HMC, sometimes worse.

Second, it seems that ESS is measured differently for different algorithms? If that's the case, how do we know those values are comparable?

Third, it seems to me that all the experiments evaluate the quality of the posterior, and none look at model evidence. Since the proposed method estimates both, I would expect to see some experiments for the latter as well.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
The paper introduces a neural network-based algorithm for learning approximate posteriors across different probabilistic programs expressed in a simple language. In contrast to prior work, the algorithm amortizes inference across different programs, rather than just across different data for the same program. This is accomplished in a white-box fashion, by having the neural network read the program source line by line, and output updated approximate posterior from a parametric family at each step. The algorithm is shown to generalize across programs with different structures.

**Requested Changes:**
With a paper like this, introducing a conceptually simple algorithm for a novel use case, the devil is in the details of the experimental evaluation. I think Section 5.3 in particular could use some clarifications, answering my questions above. I think the main programs used for evaluation should be presented in the main text, rather than the appendix.

The following is not necessary to address, but may be interesting:
The method learns both he posterior and marginal likelihood, which is accomplished by using a sum of two objectives with an arbitrary weight hyperparameter. I was wondering whether there is a trade-off between learning one versus the other, especially given a limited network size. It also seems weird to me that the loss targets an L2 loss on marginal likelihood, rather than log-marginal likelihood. The other term is the KL, which is in log-prob space.

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
No concerns

## Strengths ##
As far as I can tell, the presented results appear novel (but I am not an expert in this particular niche), and empirical results seem to suggest modest improvements in hold-out predictive performance when enforcing invariant features. I also found the example in Fig. 2 to be quite illustrative: since the gradCam explanation algorithm is not equivariant to e.g. image flipping, then the associated explanations are not. The invariant features nicely improve this situation.

## Weaknesses ##
My main concern with the paper is that I find it very difficult to read. I am not part of the intended audience, so I understand that the paper is not aimed directly at me. Yet, I had to read the paper several times to perform this review, and I still struggle with the elementary aspects of the work. Consequently, the remainder of my review will focus on highlighting places where I got stuck (see Requested Changes below).

**Summary Of Contributions:**
The paper considers learning invariant global features in convolutional neural networks. Here the considered invariance is the group of image content-preserving transformations (e.g. image flipping, 90-degree rotations, etc). Under the assumption that this group is restricted to consist of orthogonal matrices, the paper proves that a linear classifier trained on the resulting invariant features itself becomes invariant. The paper further shows how to perform PCA and k-means on these invariant features.

**Requested Changes:**
In line 3 of the introduction it states that $F = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N F(x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{global}}$. From this I deduce that $F$ is both a function $F: \mathbb{R}^{d_{local}} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{d_{global}}$ *and* a vector $F \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{global}}$. Already, at this stage, I am stuck, because those two seem to contradict each other.

The main result of the paper is Theorem 1. I found this to be highly underspecified to the degree that I do not know what the theorem shows. Specifically:
* The training data is defined as $\\{(v_m, y_m)\\}_{m=1}^M \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathcal{C}$. I assume that it's rather $(v_m, y_m) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathcal{C}$, but even so: what is $\mathcal{C}$? This space does not appear to be defined.
* The loss function $l$, can that be any function? The text seems to indicate some notion of convexity of required, but I am unable to tell from the theorem precisely what is required (if anything).
* I did not understand the meaning of the sentence:
> ... which implies that $\\{(v_m, y_m)\\}_{m=1}^M \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathcal{C}$ exhibits the same distribution as $\\{(\pi(g)v_m, y_m)\\}_{m=1}^M \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathcal{C}$ for any $g$.
(apologies for formatting; I could not get Openreview to behave)
* In the proof, I did not understand the step from the second to the third line of Eq 3.
* In the last line of Eq 3, $w^{(1)}$ and $v_m^{(1)}$ does not appear to be defined.

All in all, I do not understand the statement in Theorem 1 nor do I understand its proof. This may be an issue on my side, but I see a significant lack of precision.

As a side-remark, I enjoyed the section "Group consisting of identity mapping and image flipping" in the appendix and I would recommend that it is moved to the main paper as it eased my second reading of the paper.

*Remark:*
Below I answered No to Claims and Evidence; this answer is based on my lack of understanding of the theory. I'm happy to change this in case a more precise paper is submitted.
*update:* After having read the revised version of the paper, I have changed this to Yes as the paper is now sufficiently clear.

*Remark:*
Below I answer Yes to Audience, but this is highly speculative as I am not the intended reader group, but I naively assume one such exist.

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
I have no such concerns.

The ideas and results are presented well. The authors provided an extensive set of experimental results to support their position, including ablation studies. In general, I am convinced that the performance gains they see are real. They also provide theoretical results that support their claims in an idealistic setting.

I don't see any weaknesses that should prevent the paper from being published.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
The authors propose a method of augmenting feature maps from static or learned linear-nonlinear neural network layers to encode invariance to standard identity-preserving transformations. They provide theoretical as well as experimental support for their ideas, which together suggest that such a method can lead to improved performance over no augmentation at all. Additionally, they compare their method against augmenting training data with the same transformations, and provide results suggesting that their method achieves approximately equivalent performance with lower training time requirements.

**Requested Changes:**
**Easier:** These suggestions should be pretty easy to include in the final revision.

* You might consider how your contributions fit in with prior work from Ramakrishna Kakarala [1], Rajesh Rao [2-3], Bruno Olshausen [4-6], and colleagues. To be clear, I think your background section is quite comprehensive, as this is a fairly large research area. But in my opinion these works have carved out unique perspectives on the problem.

* You compare against augmenting the training data with the same transformations and note that your method has an improved training time. Isn't there alternatively an additional cost of combining the transformed feature representations at each activity map in your method? How do they actually compare? I think some numbers comparing the compute time or flops between the two methods would be interesting. Also, could you add a row repeating the scores of your methods without augmented training data to Table 5? This will make it easier to compare.

* I'm curious if you have a suggestion for why the accuracy trends in Table 3 are not consistent between the Test Accuracy and Augmented Test Accuracy conditions. Specifically, FMD & UIUC go up; DTD & CUB go down; and Cars stay the same.

**More involved:** These next suggestions might be a lot more work (re-running experiments; re-training networks with a new loss; implementing an alternative published analysis method). I think the paper is publication-worthy without answering them fully. However, I will leave it to the chair to require any of the changes in the context of other reviews.

* I think the standard practice for reporting ML accuracies is to report mean & variance across random seeds (e.g. for weight initialization & data shuffles). It helps to understand how much your accuracy gains. For example, Table 3 Test Accuracy for iBP on FMD is 0.08% better. Is that significant?

* I would be interested to see some more information on how you augmented the training data to obtain the results in Table 5. How does your method compare to [7]? Specifically, I'm interested to know if adding a regularization loss like they describe in eq 5 would improve the data augmentation results. [7] seems to suggest that this is necessary in addition to augmenting the data.

* I don't really see how the GradCAM results support your claims. You note that "The shape of the heatmap is relatively preserved with the proposed invariant coding method." I don't see this. The variance in the heatmap shape seems about the same between iSQRT-COV (Resnet50) (left column) and the proposed method. I didn’t notice much of a difference in the appendix figure either. Is there a way that you can quantify this? Perhaps some sort of intersection over union. You may also consider using GradCam++ [8]; the improved gradient masks might make your point more clear.

**Minor suggestions / typo edits:**

* Abstract: "explicitly consider group action" --> "explicitly considers group action"

* Bottom of page 1: "Therefore, this assumption is valid." --> I didn't follow this argument. I would appreciate it if you put a little more time into this part. It is a good section because it lays out a high-level description of your assumptions.

* Bottom of page 2, first contribution: Can you reword this contribution? We know that orthogonal perturbations to a linear classifier's weights will result in no difference in activation levels, because of linearity. I don't think this is what you're saying, but it is not clear to me how what you are saying here is different.

* Top of page 6, "Section Section 4.3" --> "Section 4.3"

* Bottom of page 13, "Table Table 8" --> "Table 8"

**Broader Impact Concerns:**

Strengths
The experiments using image recognition datasets and simple examples (for example Table 3, 4 and Figure 2) show that the proposed methods (based on invariant feature coding) are able to capture invariant image content while the baseline are not. 

Weaknesses
1. The current version of the manuscript did not provide any complexity analyses of the proposed method. It even did not state about the computational environment where the experiments were done. It is not clear how much computational resources the proposed method would take compared to existing methods.
2. The manuscript could be improved in terms of presentation. It also seems that some details about the experimental settings are missing. Please see the detailed comments in “Requested Changes”.
3. The datasets used in the experiments are not large. Even UICU data includes around 12 images per each category in average. I am not sure if this size of the data sets is large enough to validate the performance of certain proposed models in this specific research area. 


**Summary Of Contributions:**
The manuscript proposes variants of the feature coding method which calculates a single global feature by aggregating the local feature extracted from an image.  It proposes 1) group-invariant extensions of feature coding methods, including Invariant PCA and Invariant K-means, and provides 2) a proof that the optimal solution of L2-regularized convex loss minimization, i.e., a linear classifier, is group-invariant when trained on the space where the group acts orthogonally. From the experiments conducted on image recognition datasets, the proposed methods improved the recognition performance compared to the baselines which produce non-invariant features.  

**Requested Changes:**
It would be better to add formal definitions or concrete examples for some notations at the place where the notations are first introduced. For example, what would the definitions of “group representations”, “group action” and “representations” be? In addition, about “g and G” in Section 3, I think the authors could introduce the D4 groups here as examples of “g and G”.   

Minor: “\pi(g)and\sigama(g)” and “\piand\sigama”: space missing? >> “\pi and \sigama”?

It would be minor, but is not the loss in eq. (2) the form of multiclass classification losses? In linear multiclass classification, we need |C| number of weight parameters (w_{1, … ,|C|} unless the authors want to solve ordered multiclass classification problems. The descriptions are not clear enough. 
In Section 4.5 and Section 5.2, it is not clear what kind of the loss function is used here. In addition, the parameter w should be a matrix whose column size is the same as the number of classes |C|. 

About Theorem 1. 
1. What is the formal definition of “T” in the eq. (3)? 
2. It is not clear how v_m is connected to the local feature x_n. v_m is the global feature F? 
3. Please include the explicit (formal) definition of the statement “The solution of the L2-regulazed convex loss minimization is G-invariant”? 
4. “Furthermore, w^{(t)}s and x_{i}^{(t)} are orthogonal”: x_{i}^{(t)} is a typo? It was not mentioned in Theorem 1 before. 
5. It is not clear the main point of Theorem 1. It is difficult to me to connect Theorem 1 with the generalization error. Could you elaborate more about the connection between Theorem 1 and generalization error? I am also wondering how practical this connection would be. What I mean, for example, this connection really explains why the proposed method worked better than the baselines in the experimental results?

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
None

### Strengths.
1. The studied problem is quite important. The authors have clearly described the motivations.
2. The idea of bi-level optimization makes sense and is suitable for this problem.
3. The authors provided solid theoretical analysis for their method.

### Weaknesses.
I have also carefully read the reviews in the last round, and I find the last-round reviewers have some common concerns with me.

1. The scale of the experiments is limited. As mentioned above, the studied problem is very important because today's model size is very large (we must use large retained models due to their superior performance). Therefore, to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, experiments with large-model and large-scale datasets are required.
2. The proposed method is close to gradient alignment; in other words, it is based on gradient alignment without many new insights.
3. The authors still do not provide codes for reproducibility.

Overall speaking, the concerns proposed by the last-round reviewers are still unresolved. I observed two versions of manuscripts; there are not enough workloads or new high-quality changes.

This paper is about resolving the gap between pretrain tasks and the downstream task. This topic is very important, and the authors have selected a good research problem.

Strengths:
1. The paper conducts thorough experiments and interesting studies in the discussion part. Many of my concerns when reading the paper have already been addressed in the discussion.


Weaknesses:
1. Although the proposed setting could generalize many other learning schemes, the experiments are most relevant to transfer learning and domain adaptation. Experiments in different settings might be necessary to demonstrate the method's generalization to schemes such as continual learning and multi-task learning.

2. I am a bit concerned with the setting and its relationship to meta learning. It seems the practical scenario is that a large generic dataset will be available. However, in the experiments, the paper does not start from a model that is pre-trained on the generic dataset. If a new specific dataset comes, the method will need to train on the new task together with the generic dataset. If there are many different specific datasets, the problem falls under meta learning.

3. The proposed method essentially aims to identify samples in the generic dataset that share similar gradients as the specific dataset (in an online fashion during the training process). Moreover, as also pointed out in the paper, the sampling method performs worse than the top-k selection method. The intuition behind those is not well understood. It seems that the method is finding the most ''simple'' samples from the generic dataset to help the specific dataset. If there are really generic samples with very similar gradients, they probably do not give extra information in addition to the specific samples. It seems to me that samples that are similar but not the most similar are most beneficial. Moreover, the method is used as a pre-training step and a fine-tuning step on the specific task boosts the performance quite significantly. Then for a pre-training step, why is learning the ``simple'' samples beneficial?

**Summary Of Contributions:**
The paper studies the problem of learning from a limited specific dataset with a large generic data set available, which is, however, of a different distribution. The paper models the learning as a bi-level optimization problem. Particularly, the paper uses a weight model to assign weights to the generic dataset samples so that the learned weights from the weighted generic dataset give the best performance on the specific dataset. The paper applies the proposed method to three tasks and shows some improved performance.

**Requested Changes:**
Please address the weaknesses part.

Minor:
1. Why are the proposed methods called ''sparse ***'' in the result tables? 
2. I appreciate the authors' efforts, but Table 3 is still very hard to parse.

**Broader Impact Concerns:**
N/A

This submission provides a rigorous theoretical analysis; the proofs appear correct and the assumptions are clearly stated. My main concern is reproducibility: no code is provided and several hyperparameters are unreported. The related-work coverage is adequate. Overall the significance for the broader community seems modest.

Strengths:

Weaknesses:
- While the experiments are extensive, I do not think they target the right set of questions. This strikes me as an instance of "a solution in search of a problem".

**Summary Of Contributions:**
This paper proposes to improve detection of "hallucinations" in LLMs by training a family of reward models, each of which is specialized to a particular type of "hallucination". In order to do so, the authors propose a new taxonomy of hallucinations, which they argue is more fine-grained than that used in prior work. Using this taxonomy, they then generate large sets of synthetic data by injecting a specific type of hallucination into a gold-standard reasoning chain with API-served, pretrained models. The authors then train their specialized reward models independently for each subset of the data; the final score of a candidate solution is then taken to be the sum of each reward model's score. Empirically, the authors find that the overall score forms a better signal for the correctness of the solution than those of course-grained reward models, although simply prompting pre-trained models appears to be competitive in some settings.

**Requested Changes:**
- Major: Training one reward model (which, in your setting, is basically a binary classifier) per hallucination type is one way to use fine-grained data. However, you could also imagine training a single, multi-class classifier. Prior work in the code generation literature (which shares a great deal of overlap with the type of reasoning tasks you consider here) has found that the score assigned by this single model to the "no error" label is a much stronger signal than when a binary model is trained on coarse-grained data [1]. I would like to see this included as a baseline in this paper, since it's otherwise unclear what the impact is of some particularities of your setup (e.g. that you don't normalize the reward).
- Major: Per equation 6 and the preceding discussion, your formal definition of FG-PRM makes it sound like it at time $i$ only has access to the input/prompt $x$ and the current "step" $y_i$; if this were the case you could of course not detect, for example, logical inconsistencies between $y_i$ and $y_{<i}$. There thus appears to be a mismatch between your verbal explanation of FG-PRM and the formal/precise definition given, which needs to be rectified.
- Major: Section 5.3 does not make it clear what data the PRM baseline is trained on in the non-Math Shepherd setting. (Section 5.1 appears to be stating only that you use FG-H for both testing and training in the *synthetic* evaluation section?) If it is trained on FG-H then this should be stated clearly, so that the reader does not think you (for example) simply lifted the number in the table from some previous work. (If it is trained on CG-H then these results are of course meaningless, as the FG-PRM is benefitting from having access to a much larger set of training data.)
- Minor: The discussion of the evaluation on "Human-annotated Data" is not very clear. You say that you use GPT-3.5 to generate solutions for 50 problems from MATH, and then later state that each hallucination type has 50 human-annotated reasoning chains. Assuming the types in your taxonomy are meant to be distinct, that would require 6 * 50 = 300 reasoning chains. Where do the extra 250 chains come from?
- Minor: Equation (6) does not normalize the reward w.r.t. the length of the answer. It seems to me that this means that long answers with low confidence may be assigned a higher reward than short sequences with high confidence, and vice versa. I think the paper would benefit greatly from an investigation into this phenomenon and whether or not it causes issues in your setup.
- Minor: The decision to train fine-grained vs. coarse-grained reward models appears to be orthogonal to whether the reward model is outcome-based or process-based. Have you considered training "FG-ORM" models? How do you expect such a model would do, compared to FG-PRM? This would be interesting to discuss in the paper.

This paper introduces Socrates loss, a novel approach to improve deep neural network calibration by incorporating an auxiliary class and modifying the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence loss. The method encourages the network to predict the auxiliary class in uncertain scenarios by adding a dedicated regularization term. The authors provide theoretical insights demonstrating that Socrates loss serves as a lower bound of the standard KL divergence loss. Empirical comparisons with non-architectural baseline methods highlight its advantages, particularly in terms of accuracy and Expected Calibration Error.

Beyond empirical gains, I would like a clearer explanation of why this term specifically helps close the accuracy–calibration gap. In prior work, focal loss is mainly used to improve classification performance by emphasizing hard examples; its connection to confidence calibration is not obvious. The ablations in the appendix did not convincingly demonstrate that this term is necessary rather than simply beneficial in some settings. Moreover, there are presentation issues: Tables 8 and 9 appear to have incorrect bold/italic markings, which makes it harder to interpret the intended takeaways. 

Second, since the method introduces an “idk” class, it would be important to report how this behaves during training. In particular, what is the trend of the model’s probability/confidence assigned to “idk” over epochs? Showing how often “idk” is predicted over time would clarify whether it is functioning as a meaningful uncertainty mechanism or primarily acting as a regularizer. 

Third, the experimental validation feels limited in scope. The number/diversity of datasets and model architectures are relatively small for claims about general effectiveness, and additional settings (more architectures, larger-scale datasets) would strengthen the empirical case. I would suggest adding results on ImageNet and testing modern architectures such as Swin Transformer and ConvNeXt for a better analysis.

Finally, I am not convinced by the definition of GCE. Averaging (1−accuracy) with three calibration metrics mixes quantities with different scales and semantics, and the equal weighting implicitly prioritizes calibration error over accuracy without a clear justification. Either the weighting should be explicitly justified (and potentially rebalanced), or the paper should report a composite score based only on calibration metrics.

Confidence calibration is an important and broadly relevant topic, and the paper’s goal of a single objective that improves both accuracy and calibration should appeal to researchers in trustworthy ML and practical deployment. That said, the current experimental scope limits how general the conclusions feel; with stronger validation (more datasets/architectures), the findings would be more compelling to a wider portion of the audience.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
Summary of Contributions

This submissions proposes Socrates Loss, a unified training loss for deep neural network classification that tries to jointly improve calibration and classification performance, but maintaining stable optimization dynamics. This is because the authors claim (and show empirically) that there is a stability–performance trade-off in ad-hoc calibration losses: approaches with time-varying or two-stages objectives (meaning scheduled or multi-loss training) can achieve strong accuracy but often paying a price of unstable training dynamics and degrading calibration, whereas single-loss methods tend to be more stable but sometimes underperform in accuracy. This Socrates loss is designed to preserve the optimization stability of single-loss training while achieving competitive accuracy and calibration. The method introduces an auxiliary unknown class whose predicted probability intends to modulate the loss through a dynamic uncertainty penalty, allowing uncertainty awareness to be integrated end-to-end instead of through post-hoc calibration or scheduled multi-loss training. 

The paper gives an extensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets, architectures (including several CNNs and vision transformers), and training regimes, with some attention to training dynamics, convergence behavior, and calibration evolution over epochs. Ablation studies analyze the role played by the main loss components and hyperparameters, and comparisons are conducted against a wide set of ad-hoc and post-hoc calibration strategies.

Relative to the earlier ICLR submission of this work, the current version expands the experimental scope, improves clarity and organization, adds ablations and sensitivity analyses, and addresses most of the concerns previous reviewrs had regarding empirical validation and presentation. In summary, this work is mostly empirical, and contributes a comparative analysis of calibration-aware training strategies, together with a concrete loss designed to mitigate some observed instability issues.

**Claims Explanation:**
The main empirical claims of the paper are generally supported by experimental evidence. In particular, the authors demonstrate that several existing ad-hoc calibration approaches with scheduled or time-varying objectives can exhibit unstable training behavior, including sudden changes in loss and calibration metrics, and in some cases premature convergence or degradation of calibration. These observations are documented consistently across multiple datasets, architectures, and random seeds, and are supported by training-dynamics plots and per-epoch calibration analyses.

The Socrates Loss is shown to have smoother optimization dynamics while achieving competitive final accuracy and calibration compared to a range of ad-hoc and post-hoc baselines. Ablation studies support the role of the main loss components and seem to indicate that this behavior is not driven by a single design choice or hyperparameter setting. The expanded experimental coverage relative to the earlier ICLR submission, including additional architectures and transfer-learning scenarios, supports the authors' conclusions comprehensively.

That said, some claims, specifically the ones related to achieving a "state-of-the-art balance" between accuracy and calibration, rely on composite evaluation metrics the design of which raises some questions and would benefit from further clarification, please see below. In any case, the core empirical observations regarding training stability, calibration behavior, and comparative performance are well described and supported by the reported results.

**Audience Explanation:**
The findings of this paper are likely to be of interest to researchers working on model calibration, reliability, and uncertainty-aware learning, and also those using deep classifiers in settings where confidence estimates and training stability are relevant. The empirical analysis of training dynamics and failure modes of existing ad-hoc calibration methods provides useful (and probably novel) insight beyond final-epoch performance comparisons, and the proposed loss offers a concrete alternative for integrating calibration objectives directly into training. The comparative evaluation and discussion of stability issues in calibration-aware training are informative and relevant to the TMLR audience.

1) **Major: GCE metric**

The proposed General Calibration Error (GCE) raises methodological concerns that should be addressed before acceptance.

* GCE combines metrics that live on different natural scales (ECE, AdaECE, CW-ECE, and 1-accuracy) using equal weighting, without normalization or decision-theoretic justification.
* In particular, ECE and AdaECE are highly correlated estimators of the same underlying quantity  (only binning strategy changes here). This becomes quite obvious if one looks at Tables 1 and 2, where they result in nearly identical rankings: whenever a method is bold or underlined in ECE, it is also bold or underlined in AdaECE. Including both effectively double-counts the same calibration signal in an un-weighted average of four terms. This does not sound like a good idea.
* Related to this, despite the emphasis placed on GCE (with a section of its own). neither GCE nor AdaECE or CW-ECE appear to be used in hyperparameter selection or ablation analysis (see Appendix), where evaluation is instead carried out mostly in terms of accuracy and ECE alone. This implicitly treats ECE as a sufficient calibration metric, which further questions the justification for introducing and emphasizing a more complex composite metric. In other words, if the authors themselves do not use GCE for picking hyperparameters, that speaks poorly for their conviction on this being a good metric in this context.
* Indeed, Appendix C motivates the use of multiple metrics in general, but does not analyze redundancy or correlation among them, nor justify the specific choice and weighting used in GCE.

As a result, GCE is difficult to interpret as a principled evaluation criterion, and its use to support "state-of-the-art balance" claims is not really convincing, I believe. More generally, if the goal is to summarize performance across heterogeneous metrics, a ranking-based aggregation would be more appropriate than averaging raw metric values, given that the metrics involved live on different natural scales. Rank aggregation avoids arbitrary scale effects and better reflects the ordinal nature of most comparative claims made in the paper.

However, even under a ranking-based approach, there's still the need to avoid double-counting highly correlated metrics. In particular, including both ECE and AdaECE-even as ranks would still amount to overweighting the same calibration signal. A more principled aggregation, maybe, could be to restrict attention to a minimal and conceptually distinct set of metrics, most naturally accuracy and ECE (with CW-ECE included only if classwise calibration is a specific concern, this I guess might be dataset dependent?). Alternatively, the authors may wish to avoid composite metrics altogether and rely on Pareto-style or dominance-based analysis, which would be completely justified.

**Summary Of Contributions:**
This paper aims to understand the information captured by neural network representations (specifically, self-supervised learning (SSL) methods) by going beyond the standard downstream classification task, and instead visualizing the representations with a class-conditional diffusion model (RCDM). They find that this RCDM helps to uncover the fact that SSL representations are robust to adversarial perturbations and demonstrate invariance to certain kinds of transformations, though with varying degrees across SSL methods.
